title: Do look up!
caption: A fish-eye panorama of the Very Large Telescope and its laser guide stars, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory (Very Large Telescope), Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Glowing laser beams shoot up into the night from ESO’s Very Large Telescope in this fish-eye view of Cerro Paranal, deep in Chile’s Atacama Desert. French astrophotographer Martin Lefranc, who came with a group of astrophotographers in search of the darkest skies, said the sky above Paranal was “like a fever dream.”
To capture the whole scene, he took 24 separate images and combined them into one round panorama, with the telescopes standing all around its edge.

The lasers are not for show. One of the VLT’s Unit Telescopes fires them upward to make artificial stars about 90 kilometers above the ground. Watching how those “fake stars” twinkle tells the telescope how the air is churning, and a special deformable mirror then bends to cancel out the blur in real time. The technique, called adaptive optics, is crucial for sharp images from the ground, even if it makes the observatory look like a science-fiction set.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to M. Lefranc/ESO. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: A panorama combined from 24 images (source figure).

explore: Air turbulence is what makes stars twinkle. For a big telescope, that same twinkling blurs every image, so measuring it hundreds of times a second and correcting for it brings the view much closer to what a telescope in space would see.
alt: A round fish-eye view of the night sky ringed by large telescope domes, with orange laser beams reaching up from one of them toward the Milky Way.
